Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Provide emotional support and companionship to patients
Situation2: A patient is recovering from a recent surgery and appears anxious and a bit scared.
Story:
It was just past midnight when my phone buzzed, jolting me from a light doze in the staff lounge. I saw my best friend’s name flash on the screen, and when I answered, her voice was trembling, thick with tears. She could barely get the words out—her father had just passed away unexpectedly. My heart clenched. She needed me to listen, to be there, to help her hold the pieces together. I wanted nothing more than to stay on the line, to let her pour out her grief.

But as I tried to comfort her, I heard the soft chime from the patient call bell down the hall. Mrs. Lee, who’d just come out of surgery, was alone and frightened, her voice shaky as she asked for someone to sit with her. I knew she depended on me for reassurance, for a calm presence in the sterile, lonely room. My friend’s sobs echoed in my ear, while Mrs. Lee’s anxious plea tugged at my conscience. I felt torn in two, pulled by the urgent needs of two people who both counted on me for comfort, wishing I could be fully present for them both, but knowing I couldn’t.
